rationale: Start with a broad gradient to observe all 22 compounds and identify the elution window and critical pairs. A moderate temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Keep the gradient fixed and raise temperature to test selectivity changes, particularly in the late co-eluting cluster. Reduced retention may also create time headroom for a shallower gradient if needed.

Test the opposite temperature limit with the gradient unchanged, since heating worsened the early critical pair without resolving the late co-elution. This will establish whether cooling improves selectivity enough to justify subsequent gradient adjustment.

Change only gradient duration from the best run to measure slope sensitivity of the unresolved pairs. The steeper gradient also removes the time penalty and may separate the late co-elution if its components have different solvent-strength sensitivities.

Use a narrower, shallower gradient at the best temperature to improve the slope-sensitive middle and late pairs. Raising the starting organic fraction should offset the added retention time, while testing whether the earliest peaks remain adequately retained.

Further narrow the gradient to improve the remaining slope-sensitive pairs while advancing the late peaks. The early peaks have enough retention and resolution margin to test a higher starting organic fraction.

Make the gradient modestly shallower than injection 6 while retaining its starting composition. This should improve the middle and late critical pairs while keeping the last peak near, but below, 10 minutes.

Use a slightly shallower gradient, ending near the late elution window, to improve the remaining critical pairs. The final hold also tests whether changing the late solvent profile can disrupt the persistent co-elution without a substantial time penalty.

Test a substantially higher starting composition with a shallower slope to alter selectivity rather than merely stretch the chromatogram. This may improve the stubborn late cluster, while revealing whether early-pair compression limits further window trimming.

Interpolate between the strongest methods using a moderate starting fraction and a 0.05-per-minute slope. This should preserve early separation while bringing the middle critical pairs closer to full credit with the last peak near 10 minutes.

Revisit injection 8 at a moderately higher temperature to reduce its small time penalty and test selectivity under the shallower gradient. Heating may improve the middle pair while retaining the early-pair resolution gained from the higher starting composition.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 8 but a higher endpoint, eliminating its late hold-related delay. This targets full credit for the middle pairs while keeping the last peak close to 10 minutes.

Test a faster gradient followed by a moderate-organic hold, placing the persistent late cluster in a different solvent regime. The low starting fraction protects early retention, while the 0.65 endpoint has already demonstrated complete elution.

Test a slightly shallower gradient near the best method, with modest heating to offset the added retention time. This probes whether improved slope-dependent separation outweighs the small selectivity losses seen on heating.

Refine around injection 12 with a slightly steeper gradient that should put the last peak safely below 10 minutes. This tests whether removing its time penalty preserves enough resolution to improve the best score.

Test a distinct selectivity regime: a rapid gradient followed by a lower-organic hold, so more of the mixture separates during the hold. This may break the persistent late co-elution that has barely responded to temperature or shallow-gradient adjustments.

Test the remaining intermediate starting composition with a shallower gradient designed to keep the last peak near 10 minutes. This checks whether gains in the late cluster can outweigh compression of the early and middle critical pairs.

Raise temperature just one step from injection 12 to remove its small time penalty. Keeping the gradient unchanged will test whether the resulting selectivity trade-off improves the score near the current optimum.

Test a slope between injections 5 and 10 at the lower starting composition, which better preserves the middle-pair selectivity. The endpoint remains high enough to avoid the delayed final hold seen with 0.65 organic.
Test a single temperature step above the best method while holding its gradient fixed. This isolates whether modest selectivity changes can improve the score without introducing a time penalty.

Test a lower starting fraction with a compensating steeper slope, targeting a last peak near 10 minutes. This checks whether improved middle-pair selectivity can outperform the higher-starting-fraction methods.

Test a slightly shallower slope than injection 12 to improve the remaining middle and late pairs. The expected small time penalty will establish whether additional resolution can outweigh crossing the 10-minute boundary.

Raise injection 22 by one temperature step to recover most of its time penalty while retaining its shallower slope. This tests the remaining local trade-off between improved resolution and the 10-minute cutoff.

Test a slightly shallower gradient at the lower starting fraction, using moderate heating to keep the last peak near 10 minutes. This targets the favorable middle-pair separation seen in injection 19 while reducing its time penalty.

Test the intermediate temperature between injections 8 and 11, aiming to remove the late-hold time penalty while limiting the selectivity losses observed at 35 C. This is a final local refinement near the strongest gradient slopes.
